paras: The White Cap threat against Burr McCowan was a postal card signed "White Caps" that threatened McCowan, a young Black letter carrier in Delaware, Ohio, with death on December 4, 1888, for being a Democrat. No violence followed, and McCowan and local officials treated the card as a joke. Newspapers across the country carried the story as part of reports that the White Caps had reached Ohio.

The card arrived amid a run of warning notices signed "White Caps" in Ohio and Kentucky towns that week. On the same day a Columbus man named Welch received a White Cap letter threatening him with the blacksnake whip for drinking and abusing his family.

According to a Delaware dispatch, the card passed through the mail window at the post office on the morning of December 4, addressed to McCowan. It was decorated with a rudely drawn whip and threatened his life, the charge against him being "a Negro Democrat." As printed in the wire story, it read: "No negro Democrats allowed to hold office. Choose ye Republicanism or death. Beware of White Caps. Dead men tell no tales."

McCowan was reported to look on the matter as a joke and to be "not in the least worried," a view officials and many others were said to share. The Delaware correspondent described him as an honest, industrious young man whom everyone respected, "his greatest weakness being his politics," and said the town laughed at the card as the act of "a would-be funny idler." No report of the sender being identified or arrested appears in the coverage.

The story spread on December 5 and 6 through a Columbus wire item that paired McCowan's card with the Welch letter. Headlines stressed the movement of the White Caps rather than McCowan: the St. Paul Daily Globe wrote that "The Terrors of Indiana Propose to Do Business in Ohio," and the Rock Island Daily Argus ran "Buckeye White-Caps Are Bold." Papers in Lancaster, Wilmington, Waterbury and Kansas printed the same text, and shorter versions identified McCowan as "a colored Democrat."

The Cleveland Gazette printed the separate Delaware dispatch on December 8 in its column of Ohio and Pennsylvania community news, under the heading "Ohio's Ku Klux—The White Caps." That account added the drawn whip and the praise of McCowan's character, while still dismissing the card as a prank.
Papers printed the victim's surname as McCowan, McGowan and, in one short version, "Bever McCowan"; the Delaware report and most wire copies use McCowan.

accounts.label: Columbus wire report
accounts.gist: McCowan received a postal card purporting to come from the White Caps ordering 'Republicanism or death'; he looked on it as a joke and was not worried.

accounts.label: Delaware local dispatch
accounts.gist: The card, decorated with a drawn whip, threatened his life for being 'a Negro Democrat'; the town laughed at it as the work of an idle prankster.

framing.detail: Papers from Minnesota to Delaware ran the Columbus story under headlines such as 'Warned by White Caps' and 'White Caps Invade Columbus', framing it as the Indiana White Caps spreading into Ohio.
Short versions called McCowan 'a colored Democrat' and said officials shared his view that the card was a joke.
The Cleveland Gazette headed the item "Ohio's Ku Klux—The White Caps" but printed a local dispatch that praised McCowan and dismissed the card as a prank.

conflicts.note: Most versions, including the Delaware local report, print McCowan; the Globe uses both spellings in one item, and 'Bever' is likely an OCR or typesetting error.
